My entire team is suffering with in the first 3 months of joining.  Note: If you are not a techie, please do a proper enquiry about the team & the management before joining. Since there are teams at IBM which respects employees, if you are joining those teams, well and good. All the best.

Pros: Flexible hours, no micromanagement, respect, fun people to work with, if you are highly motivated this place will be good to you.
Cons: for a processdriven organization, some processes are dreadful... took me a week to get a new mac when mine stopped working... need an adapter for an external screen.. its been 2 weeks and still, they are working out a correct cost code it needs to be billed to.. 69 euros worth!?. The bullying policy is not existing if your manager is a friend with the second line manager... 4 people complained to HR about one specific manager and noting has been done about it.

Pros: The only upside is the flexibility to "work from home"...
Cons: Although the socalled "work from home" flexibility, this organisation crawls it back effectively by dishing out the worst pay increment/ performance bonus yearonyear based on my experience with them for the past 4 years given the fact that my performance rating is consistently on a "AboveAverage Contributor" 2+, whereby a 1 rating is considered top performer. So is this really considered an employee benefit or simply paying out of pocket for this flexibility?? In addition, I am expected to clock in minimum of 40 hours training per calendar year with ZERO training budget. This is the biggest joke thus far that I come across.... And what counts into the training hours? Team meetings, internal socalled "cross trainings".... which are not creating a positive impact to my career growth in anyway. This is on top of the everdemanding work environment that I am placed into, while working with team members from across the other regions.

Pros: At least outside USA, IBM is easy to get hired: good for newbbies, old people that want something relaxed although it forces you to live in a cheap country. You can negotiate HO and in general real technical workload is little. Is a good move to start just for 1 year or to go there for a relax preretirement taking advantage that most of the staff is newbbie.
Cons: A Burocracy hell, with a proportion of  7 non technical roles per technician. You have to deal with painful tools to work and nobody knows in general. Documentation is lost, outdated or never done.  It seems that each team/region works in each own way with the tools they want and are not the same for all offices across the world. Low salaries, low workload, low expectations. Unless is your final stage of your career, leave before 2 years.

Pros: Inclusivity. My Austism was not an issue it actualls helps in my job. IBM understands the value that all types of people bring to the organisation. The different perspectives that peolple view the world from are all valuable to IBM.  I really feel that what I say and do will be listened to. That my views are relevant. Collaboration and peer reviews are very important here. We all learm from it and become better people.  I am currently a virtual IBMer due to CoVid19 and us all working from home. The 'onboarding' process into IBM went very smoothly. The use of video, screensharing and other collaborative tools, has delivered training, mentoring and social meetings. IBM has exploited these online colloborations to the full.
Cons: I have not been into my lab nor met my team in person. Not IBM's fault, but CoVid19. Evertything here is better than I could have hoped for. Well done IBM.

Pros: 1. Very wide product portfolio. Can learn almost everything in software world if you wish 2. Good work life balance 3. Friendly environment 4. Switching between roles is relatively easy
Cons: 1. Over last few years IBM/ISL has gone down in pay ladder. Below market salary  2. Company prefers Lateral hiring in  senior positions rather than promoting internal people  3. Over the years management is losing transparency and fairness. Still better than market but it's deteriorating rapidly  primarily owning to lateral recruitment in management cadre from  other companies. These people mostly don't know IBM values.  4. Do not expect great salary hike. IBM thinks the flexibility they are giving you must be compensated by low salary. HR simply don't care 'bout high attrition.

Pros: Flexible working culture. Good work from home options. Good brand value and lot of projects. good for Women employees. good growth opportunities  conditions apply
Cons: no transport provided  except for shifts. no free tea/coffee. No outings/ fun activities . Rarely team outings or company outings. Tough to get hikes almost impossible and very less salary growth. lot of politics . need to be really good at communication and interaction skills else you will have to take back seat. You have to be innovative because, when you come to IBM, you will find difficulty to find things starting from stationary to documentation and information in your project. work culture here is totally different so it could take time to understand and adjust. You need to be really good inorder to survive in IBM.

Pros: The people who work at IBM are terrific.  Bright, savvy, 'whatever it takes'.  I have never met a better group of dedicated professionals eager to make their clients happy.
Cons: 1. Too many Resource Actions RAs aka layoffs.  The latest round affected too many good people that IBM cannot afford to let go 2. Some ie Cringley have predicted that 78% of IBM US personnel will be gone by 2015 in order to meet the $20 EPS promise that Palmisano made, called Roadmap 2015.  Internally we call it Roadkill 2015. 3. Company manages by cost cutting and with little consideration for the people.  Do not expect any raises once you get here.

Pros: a ability to convince your cux: why IBM? why NOW? why YOU?? b a sales he or she need to have very creative view: how win/ how to grow market/ alternative approach to cux  c ability to lead brandsales product sales to listen your direct: how to win every biz oppty? d ability to tell your management a story: your territory is promising & able to achieve quota.
Cons: a Sales quota too challenging: like my team is at least 150% growth rqst from top down SMB  b management style: very pushing/ very challenging: drive you to the limit!! c matrix sales system often cause conflict & many confusion from the clients d sales too short lifecycle: change sales or change territory

Pros: Regular consulting work Pros.  A lot of resources, but no help in using it
Cons: Reliane on others to target and win business.  If they are wrong all suffer.

Pros: Work from home. Good career opportunities, if you play your cards right. Excellent work life balance. I got lucky that I could work with some really smart people, but that was just luck. Good work if you want it. They seemed more ethical than your average company. Decent job security but not too much. That's a good thing. People behave well here, unlike places where too much job security means people think they can get away with anything. Bad behaviour will get you fired here. Nice managers usually, they're usually techically sound which is important for a tech company.
Cons: Very low pay You can't work from office in IBM even if you want to. They're indirectly geared towards pushing employees to work from home.  Poor office infra, slow internet, no free tea/coffee plus you'll need to walk, climb stairs a lot to get some horrible tea and snacks. You can't work as a programmer with the cheap 8gb ram  laptops they provide, you'll need to ask for a better laptop. It's a long process.

Pros: No work load if your backeting your manager u will happy and you can enjoy , no hick no grow ,
Cons: 1. You will become very lessy   2. IBM will never use your knowledge on right way. Never give chance to grow 3. Some of the project top management will alway cheeting client   but giving workng info save there work or commitment. 4. Due to this one day they will loose the projects its better to alway top managemet has to review on ground level people  5. When the escalation  come then only every one will Wakeup till that no respect or value to tech people   6. Alway thinks PM , DOMs are respected but tech people never given motivations , recognition , Who has good knowledge he will become soon lezz..  If you not not getting respective your knowledge and no motivation dont stay will longer with IBM..

Job Title: Customer Service And Technical Support Representative
Pros: good health benefits. Possibility to access thousands of online trainings if your position allows you free time. Chance to train and move internally as long as there is no hiring freeze. Chance of promotion if you are liked by the right people and have a little conscience. Chance to work in an international environment. Highly structured HR department.
Cons: They are very cheap and stingy. No benefits beside healthcare. Little meritocracy in promotions. Higher ups and team leaders insist on preaching about company values but they are the first to misbehave when it suits them. During hiring freeze you are expected to divide the work of 12 people among 5 with no extra benefit to offset it. There was so much to do we sometimes barely went to the toilet and were reprimanded when we did. Lots of broken promises. Disorganization among different departments and lack of communication that resulted in customer dissatisfaction.

Pros: IBM is undoubtedly the best company I worked in my life. Not only it reinforces the culture of trusting and empowering the employees, but also foster us to keep learning, trying new things, experimenting, and innovating. We don't fear to make mistakes, as IBM values who tries new ways of doing things, as long as aligned to our strategy, mission and values.
Cons: Hard to find something, but if I have to pick one, it would be the fact that we are so many people, that we need to fight fiercely to be noticed out of our internal organization. But, this is not that bad, as it forces us to increase our network, and be eager to show our ideas and work. I am very proud of being an IBMer.

Pros: Some residual prestige associated with the name. I honestly thought I could find more to say than this, but I can't.
Cons: Poor executive management, largely there to maximise personal gain before leaving. Most do not believe 'the strategy' will work and don't care. Cowardly managment chain, not prepared to challenge obvious stupidity or without the stomache/dedication for a fight. Many are just trying to get in as many paydays as they can and have also lost belief. Hardnosed, naval gazing HR who churn out unpopular and irrelevant initiatives, hence consuming even more of the precious time which employees no longer have.. Pervasive self preservation rather than team cooperation to serve the customer. Tick sheet/ call centre/low cost centre mentality, even where totally inappropriate, leading to 'hidden' extra costs to solve problems Broken and massively discredited performance appraisal system, now almost completely hijacked for other purposes.. Professional judgement, constructive challenge and considered 'risk taking'  suppressed.

Pros: IBM covers just about everything in IT, many 'companies within companies'. DIY attitude to career development, which suits me to an extent. Technology is big at IBM, you can still have a fulfilling technical career at IBM getting harder... I have me a lot of great people at IBM, and most are still working there eight years later.
Cons: Huge company so... Lots of process Slow moving, slow to change Slave to the stock market, which is tough given how hard it is for IBM to change direction For a company making a lot of money, they do not splash it around.  Stock market I guess. Innovation is becoming more and more difficult due to process, but I think that affects all large organisations. Going through a tough time at the moment, trying to work out what IBM really stands for with all these new IT companies surfacing every year/month.

Pros: Learning opportunities are only limited by the number of hours in the day Great community and lots of fun social activities and opportunities to meet colleagues Huge opportunities to grow and take on responsibility; you will get recognition but you will not be compensated  Very young with lots of people from diverse educational backgrounds Very international; primarily Dutch but lots of Englishspeakers Flexible working hours when not on strict client project You can turn down a project if you don't think it's an area you want to develop in
Cons: Below market wages No pension options Expensive healthcare options No company car despite sometimes lots of travel No overtime only "time for time"  You can turn down projects, but you have to minimize your time nonbillable hours otherwise it will look bad on your annual review To find good and interesting projects, you really have to advocate for yourself

Pros: IBM is a HUGE company. Some of my coworkers use to say that there are 18 IBMs inside IBM, considering its size. Due to that, it is amazing to see how many different points of view are present in each team. That diversity is core to adapt, evolve and innovate, also bringing with it a high number of career opportunities. Not to mention that we deal, or know people who deal, with technologies that will be of a great impact in the future of humankind – and that is extremely motivational: to be part of the future.
Cons: As IBM is a very old company, there are a few legacies that are not that good: Some people, often in management roles, with old mindsets or internal systems that run in old technology, for example. But I see these things as something already being addressed by the company in different scales: through hiring young talented professionals; investing in executive coaching and other mindsetchanging activities; hiring more people to change internal process for something new and better.

Pros: Been working in IBM for the last 13 years and here comes the Pros: 1 The best part is most of the managers are easily approachable regarding any problem and they always try to help the employee. 2 You are encouraged to speak your mind and share ideas freely. 3 Always encourage you to learn more via IBM's inhouse course materials. 4 IBM has a huge repository of tools and apps and you can easily pick up one and start learning about it for free to enhance your skills. 5 Appreciates employee's effort in various channels. 6 Adapting latest tools and technologies to steer ahead in the market. 7 Flexible to Work from Home
Cons: There is no company in the world without any cons and also it depends on the employee's perspective and mindset. The few ones are: 1 Uses some old fashioned tools but the good part is IBM is discarding the old ones slowly and adapting the latest tools and apps. 2 The turn around time for some internal processes takes more time than usual. 3 Bonus payment can be better.

Pros: Expectations are very clear and information about how the company is doing overall are always communicated by senior management on a regular basis.  Compensation always seems very fair and you generally know exactly why the decisions regarding your compensation have been made.
Cons: Many of the software products developed by IBM are less than exciting.  There are very few products that are truly cutting edge.  For someone who wants to be working with the latest technologies I would recommend making sure that you will be working in an area that holds interest for you.  In addition, different parts of the company tend to be very insulated.  Moving from one area to another can be difficult mostly just because you don't really know what's happening in other teams management has no problem with people moving around.

Pros: Perks, IBM Brand, Resources to get the jobs done and marketing support.
Cons: Negotiate hard in regards to salary, or it will NOT go up. Maybe 2% to 4% per year and that is a maybe. Do not go in with an attitude, "do it and if I am wrong, I will get my hand slapped later," because people will get fired for that. Extremely rigid. Very high pressured and very management top heavy. Huge websphere presents in the management chain, so they push transactional sales and not solution selling. As a result, no room for developing territory. They continually change and move territory every year. Commission plan, you will not get paid until you hit 55% of your target and the draw you get if you choose to get it is very low.

Pros: Good management.  Reasonable pay, and room for advancement.  Great benefits.  I would recommend working here if you want the chance to find your IT specialty and have the opportunity to move.
Cons: You can get stuck in one position and find it very hard to move out, you need to do a lot of work outside of work to advance your career, off time learning and taking courses to branch into a new field.  You need to play office politics, the better you schmooze the faster you move up.

Pros: The people are IBMs biggest asset. I have worked with some great people in a lot of different teams over the last few years. There is always a focus on networking and we are pushed to expend our netwrks inside and outside IBM. This has opened up career opportunities to me that wouldn't be there if I hadn't made the effort.  There is always plenty of room to grow your career and due to IBMs size, there is a huge range of roles you can work towards.
Cons: Constant pressure on offshoring and redundancies is threatening to ruin the companies staff morale. Once we get on with the work the job can be fun, but what was once a huge IT company is now seeming run by accountants.

Pros: Informal hierarchy. You can talk easily with your manager or other senior staff and be transparent and honest.  Good technical support from the team and the manager.  Supportive and friendly atmosphere.  Good integration and socialising events.  Possibility of working from home on single days on request.
Cons: To much procedures, which makes work time consuming even when you want to implement a simple change.  Too tight specialisations, where you are not exposed for the wider technology areas. This makes it harder to see a bigger picture and understand IT infrastructure as a complete system, especially when you just start your career.  Sometimes overloaded with tasks, as for example the day before your holiday when you need too handover your tickets to other people. Moreover the same tickets get back to you after the holiday.  Not competitive salaries and no pay raises.

Pros: Benefits were good. I found that having half a dozen different disinterested people to report top meant I had a high degree of freedom in what I did. If you are in a client facing roles there are a lot of opportunities, if you are internal you are doomed as you will only be seen as a cost.
Cons: Completely numbers driven organisation which is reflected at every level.  I found it impossible to move from an internal to a client facing role  internal nonfee earning roles have the lowest status. I never had any meaningful discussion about my future with any of my many managers. I had almost no training in 7 years there. I found a general pervasive state of depression among IBMers  this of course may not be true everywhere but it was my experience. This was likely influenced by having an internal role and   by seeing many internal roles offshored to cheaper locations

Pros: Work remotely Time off when needed Good benefits People who work hard to accomplish insane deadlines
Cons: 1% annual pay raises and minimal bonuses are a disincentive to produce at a high level. There is no skills development or real training. You are just expected to know how to do everything and projects are assigned as such. Most of the Project Executives have no patience and rarely  communicate praise, only expectations. The few job title or band promotions that exist come with no or minimal salary adjustments. Seems like Sam is only interested in his stock price because it is toed to his compensation. The rest of us get nothing. Thanks Sam. Really appreciate it.

Pros: Plenty of opportunities to change roles gaining valuable experience if you have the right strategy.  However if you're stuck in 1or 2 roles and stay there for too long, don't expect much as your transferable skills will be IBM specific. Not many companies use IBM tools, defo not Lotus Notes.  Good redundancy packages!!!!!
Cons: PBC process is to make sure you work hard, but it deprives you from your bonus, salary increases, promotions and so on. If you disagree with your rating and most ppl do and you have a strong case to prove that you're right  open HR case. They might give you 2+ instead of 2, but no salary increase to complement it. Nobody will know about it, as you're not suppose to discuss PBC ratings with anyone. It is extremely biased, promotes cronyism and low morale etc. Don't complain, just be happy to have a job!!!!!

Pros: It has stature and repute, a seemingly forward looking culture and a professional management that is seemingly competent; at least that's how it looks from the outside.
Cons: It's quite different once you're inside.  For one, management didn't have clear and defined requirements of my job when they were hiring, which in retrospect it has misrepresented the job role and content at the point when I signed up for the job.

Pros: Great team of people  Good exposure to client facing roles  Remote working at task managers discretion  Good place to start your career
Cons: Not a career for the long term future.  Must be flexible and willing to travel to take on other roles you may not even want to have any chance of progression.  Targets solely based on utilisation.   Lack of benefits despite introducing pension, child care vouchers and cycle to work scheme.  Increased quantity of promotion bands limit pay rises.  Unbelievable levels of bureaucracy.   Lack of promoting any form of networking within the wider company to get on a project or role you want  due to CIC politics.  Top level management only interested in progressing themselves and achieving KPIs to get annual bonus.  Business based on ‘Cost’ model, meaning the cheaper, the better.

Pros: Within IBM there is a huge possibility for growth depending on your networking skills and how eager you are to grow and own your career. The Graduate Program, which I am a part of, has a huge platform for training and the higherups are also very involved with the growth of the early professionals graduates and apprentices. There is a lot of exposure to various projects and opportunities to build good client relationships.   The work culture is overall a good one where the people you interact with are there to support you and in essence build relationships with.
Cons: As IBM is a very huge company, once you get past the Graduate Scheme, there is a high chance career growth stagnates and you become lost in the company as there might not be as much focus on how you progress.

Pros: Atmosphere was relaxed, colleagues helpful. Pluralsight access and also Safari books and other training opportunities. In the team there were initiatives to inspire people to develop better coding practices or prepare some training. Also if someone would like to get access to some extra RPA tool it was sometimes possible to have it arrange so they could learn extra tool
Cons: In my case communication was the reason why I left this job. I had a feeling I got stuck in a rut and there is no possibility of change for any better. I think a lot of people leaves due to this factor. There is no clear vision of the future in terms of what projects will be available etc.

Pros: You can access and use IBM's best analytics tools, through Blue Opportunities you can get involved in other interesting projects  as your daily job is usually boring it is really up to you how much you use the benefits of above options.  Home office is quite common  which is s very good benefit too.
Cons: jobs controlled by processes and due to the size of the company, you get a small part of the whole process  like a manufacturing plant, so you really need to make extra efforts to find what you would like  compensation packages are below market averages  personal evaluation is based on relative measures  so if there is anyone in your global team who found better in your area, you will not get the annual raise even if you are the best expert in your country or local site, no matter how hard you try

Pros: Innovation, Watson, Client Success. IBM gives lot of importance to appreciate right people who does the right work at right time, which would give lot of confidence and satisfaction to the people who always committed to give 100% effort for the organization and the project.
Cons: Processes need to be adjusted as per the way or in situations while dealing with different clients as satisfying the client is utmost priority  for any organization, I feel sometimes bringing our complex process if any, may not be better always as some clients wouldn't be interested to follow process, meeting deadlines is only priority for those clients, so dealing with those clients, our process need to be altered bit to ensure client and organization are on the same page.

Pros: At IBM the managers and people really take car of their employees. IBM has great benefits and it is a great place to learn how a Big company works. As a Technical Sales Person they will always give you training and they will make sure you have everything you need to do your job. The Payment is good.
Cons: The Management from IBM oldest people believe IBM is the Best at everything and does not realize that their products are not the best, So when you do not make the target sales they will put the fault on you and not on the "old" product you are selling. Now IBM is changing and innovating but they are not doing it as fast as AWS, Microsoft or Google, so the Cloud business is pretty tough, you will have to provide really innovative and new ideas on how to position IBM's products to be able to make them look better than the competition.

Pros: You work with teams of contractors which are people brought from IBM Romania, from locations with abusive managers in top high management like Timisoara. You have tons of responsibility on the project and any issue raised as a problem regarding what is happening on the team gets to be blamed on you
Cons: Change the management from top position to the bottom ones for this location and for Timisoara's also. Abusive behaviour not solved or listened by HR. Lots of students and people with no experience employed and left on the project with you, just so in the end you would be accused of bad performance.  Many employees are not even online on messaging channels but you are to blame for any task postponements. You cannot have managers with 20 years of experience in IBM and still ignore the signs. Very abusive and chaotic old management

Pros: Allows you to build a great foundation in IT product knowledge, solution selling, sales forecasting and account management. The training opportunities are plenty. It's a great stepping stone for a sales career and will open many doors.
Cons: All the entry level lead general sales positions are contractbased. It's very hard to get promoted to a regular hire  virtually takes forever. Hiring managers may give you the impression that promotions come by more often than they actually do. The salaries are rather low compare to the work you do and not competitive at all with other IT companies. Bonus structure rather than commission limits your earnings.

Pros: A Global company  that gives the freedom to learn and move laterally or vertically. The amount of learning made available some of them with a cost is UNparalleled. The push to capture ideas, internal learning, sharing best practices and recognition for the same has never been more intense.
Cons: The constantly increasing pressure to deliver in an environment of UNexplained cost cuts has dampened a lot of enthusiasm and drive to work "for" the company.  Although I've not lost faith in the company's goal or working in IBM a thing of pride, the environment down under is enough to kill most people's respect, can't blame them for moving out.

Pros: There are excellent technical folks within the corporation.  These individuals are the "Real" drivers behind some of the new and innovative opportunities.  IBM financial group knows/understands how to manipulate the stock buyback process, during a downturn in the economic times, to keep the stock artificially inflated.  Great place to get experience out of college for only the first 2 years.
Cons: Currently there is no direction or guidance from the Senior Leadership positions.  The Senior management level is so removed from the customers and work being provided, that the company no longer has/or is following their own guidelines.  Outsourcing is the greatest buzz word with senior management, which is viewed as the "Magic Bullet" for their success.  Over the past 15 years, IBM has slowly been loosing market share.  In order to keep the balance sheet positive, they have had to sell off some of the most lucrative business towers: PC Division and Federal Services Division.

Pros: If you have good technical abilities you will get exposure to large and varied environments. If you have good skills and that includes negotiation skills then you can get decent pay too.  There are some nice people there and good managers.
Cons: Work is farmed offshore to lower skilled workers, as a result I spent large amounts of time cleaning up major issues created by others.  Excessive redtape and bureaucracy  No work/life balance, checkin/checkout mentality, permanents get no overtime and "time off in lieu" is rarely used and never equal to the overtime taken.  too many politics and bullying is not stopped in the workplace

Pros: 1. You get an opportunity to work on your corner of interest, even though you are working on some thing else. How? You can opt for some stretch assignment and explore new skills or work on your choice/interest of skill set.  2. You get an opportunity to showcase your skills and achievements. How? Lot of paper presentations, patents, Technical events held within IBM  3. Growth in career is easy at IBM. How ? Lot of Certifications and online courses are available within IBM. Also adapting to new skills and opportunities to implement the same are easy in IBM 4. Employee friendly environment. How? Flexible timings, work from home/remote location options
Cons: 1. Technical events do happen but the entry to other IBMers is limited due to number constraint. So only a few get a chance to attend these events. We need more such events and should be open to more IBMers.

Job Title: God Only Knows People Make Up Anything
Pros: some mates sick leave and you'll need it if you get stressed, overworked, underutilised
Cons: Virtually no benefits No formal training just a 2 hour how to setup your PC do your timesheets and read mail No R&D No Innovation Lied to about the size of bonus pool when insourced told Par was 6% Low Morale Staff are only kept to drain knowledge to offshore Entire teams of contractors let go Overtime not paid at all lucky to take time of in lieu IBM Assumes you are there for support Forced to have a mobile paid for self if contractor to be contactable for support Cost saving is the top priority of company No computer mouse, docking station, monitors are provided Managers typically have 40 people under them Manager may be in a different city 1000 km away No training No onthejob learning The be all and end of is CIRATS and SHC Poor Culture No pay increases PBC system is about whoyouknow and schmooze with NO interest from management in Career development Survivors left wondering when the axe will fall Useless office tools assuming you're not running Linux, in which case it's worse Management and PMs are mostly useless some exceptions What do DPEs do? Clients are overbilled for incompetent work

Pros: Colleagues whilst I still have them are among the best I have ever worked with.  All are loyal employees, who want to do the best for the customer
Cons: CEO, VP's, Executive Managers, L2 Managers are roadblocks to allowing the staff to function on a day to day basis without the spectre of the axe over our heads.  Job security is non existent, major only concern is employing the cheapest in the market they can, without any regard to ability.  Standards of 'post sales technical support' are suffering hugely with IBM's rush to 'offshore'.  Customer are beginning to see through the thin veil of in country support, and are increasingly frustrated with 'time to fix' becoming an ever distant line.  respect  doesn't exist payrises  ? Review process  PBC was massively broken.  Replacement Checkpoint  no better same product essentially, but with different name

Pros: Unique opportunity for research within a semicooperate environment, where projects range from fundamental research to product prototype/proof of concept.  Colleagues are world class researchers with very diverse background and always happy to chime in with their expertise.  I was grateful for the choice of using gnu/linux on the company laptop. The facility was topnotch, especially the cafeteria  if it wasn't for the early closing time 16:00, then again one could argue that this is done in order to promote healthy worklife balance. ;
Cons: IBM is truely a venerable company. Unfortunatly this implies that there is a lot of regulation for various things. While I felt that in Resarch a lot of effort is being made to circumvent this, the sheer size of the company can be felt in the amount of rules and regulations.  However, once I was accustomed to said regulation did not bother me as much as in the beginning.

Pros: Very nice pack of perks and in some areas, flexibility for Home Office. However, this flexibility changed a lot starting mid 2016, where thousands of employees were pulled back into the offices. Depending on your network, you can explore various career paths within the company.
Cons: Huge bureaucracy, inefficient processes and it's very hard to get a promotion specially being a GBS/GTS employee in the short/medium term.

Pros: Working for IBM is working for one of the most innovative and successful technology leaders, who is around for over 100 years by now. The brand name is established well and their smarter planet initiative reached beyond the technology savvy audience. Inventions such as IBM Watson excites not just geeks and science nerds, but society. All in all IBMers are proud to work for the "Big Blue".
Cons: IBM is to big to even know what the company is doing all over the world, as a "regular" employee at least. Many internal processes and tools are used to run  to many for some. Products and services sold could be easily used inside IBM, but I guess to implement things at a worldwide level and such a diverse scale of employees and management takes time.

Pros: An OK place to work for sometime and learn but don't get sucked into the processes and work culture.  The brand looks good on your resume.  If you have a good manager, you can have the opportunities to explore and look for opportunities outside your current role if you are looking for a change.
Cons: With a very strong focus on meeting numbers, employee welfare takes a backseat.  Most managers are just numbers focused and don't really care about the development of people.  Salary and hikes are bad and don't meet industry standards.  Work culture is quite political and unprofessional.  Managers are encouraged and trained to only manage numbers  Too any processes and legacy systems  don't get fooled by the focus on cutting edge technologies. None of it is implemented in the organization.

Pros: If you get the right project will be challenging, you will be able to learn lots because there is people working there that are really smart.  The tools of the company such as learning tools, career paths are well defined if you are into growing within the company.
Cons: The salary at the beginning could be competitive but you will not increase the income for years.  The visibility its really narrowed to your position so growing takes lots of time.  The yearly reviews some times are made not taking in account all the work you did or you are compared with people with other skillset and other positions that makes sometimes a disadvantage.

Immediatemanagement don't have the time to actually support their team in career development, as they have a fulltime job to do and being a people manager is just an additional task on the side.  Finally, they're offshoring everything. They have a 60/20/20 vision aka 60% resource farshore India, 20% nearshore Slovakia/Bratislava and 20% onshore UK. Not only do remote colleagues not have the skills to stepinto the shoes of those they are replacing in the UK and by replacement I mean maderedundant, but the cultures don't support each other. In the UK, employees work longhours until the job is done. In India, colleagues don't know how to think outside of a process or list of instructions for e.g. if something goes wrong and the way around it isn't on the process list then they will just stop and not do anything, they won't even come back and tell you it's not working. You will be constantly chasing them. In eastEurope, if it's 17.01 they go home. So be prepared to have to work double hard to cater for the slack elsewhere. In addition, the IMI service in India is fairly new, about 3yrs old. This means that the colleague skills are way belowpar and still being trained. About 70% of my stress was caused by IMI's inability to complete a job.  If you want to work for a company that is all about the business and dollar signs, IBM is for you. If you want a great culture, progression and support  find somewhere else. p.s. There's no free tea/coffee  you even have to pay 25p for hot water. Just to show you how low these guys go to save a buck...

Pros: 1. Worklife balance: Work culture is that of a stereotypical "government" office/ product manufacturing facility wherein only the BAU work product holds any value. As long as that can be achieved, no personal time investment is required.  2. Rest and relaxation for Big4 consultants or otherwise stressed workforce: IBM is currently written as of Oct, 2022 in nascent stages of building a consulting practice. However, the required expertise is still years away personal opinion based on 5 years of work experience in IBM and 6 years prior in a Big4 consulting organization. As such, someone coming from a highstress work environment will be able to achieve high results with minimal effort. There is ofcourse a catch, but in my personal opinion, it's worth the mental peace I'm doing this on a light Tuesday afternoon as recommended by the feedback email from the firm, go figure!.  3. Work from anywhere: If your project allows it mostly does, IBM gives you the freedom to work from anywhere, quite literally. Unsurprisingly robust network and very high performance machines deployed across all levels. It also happens to be the primary reason for IBM facing near nodowntime during the pandemic.
Cons: 1. Career stagnation: Goes without saying  easy work life comes at a steep price. Herd deployment and treatment, in terms of individual expression of workforce on projects leading to zero visibility is common.  2. Learning stagnation: Any and all levels in IBM, below may be a level 9/10 10 being the highest, BAU remains a "loop" for as long as you are present in a role which not only gets monotonous, but strips individuals of any potential to learn.  3. Pseduo management levels: No "manager" below a level 9, is a real manager. They have no authority over anything of value such as project allocations, level progressions or even project assignments and are often more helpless than their DRs i.e., if at all they are even concerned about the latter's well being. The most common response is  "may be you should discuss with xyz", where xyz is someone higherup the manager's org chart the person with any real say.  4. Mechanical leadership: IBM is a centennial organization and so are its management formulas of carrotandstick motivation. Other than generic mass mailers/town halls, there's no potential for learning with anyone from the actual leadership group. The idea of mentorship does not exist in IBM.  5. Conditional progressions: A common "loophole" presented to most IBMers by their management albeit slyly is progression against certifications. Its key to note that even with progressions, your work profile or BAU rarely changes.  6. NOT RECOMMENDED FOR THOSE JOINING FROM THE IT INDUSTRY  Are you working in Infosys, Wipro, TCS, Accenture, Microsoft et. al., considering a move to IBM for a better career etc.? Then, please don't. IBM will most likely give you same environment that you just quit. You may land a significant raise in compensation at the time of joining, but that'll be normalized out with minimal increments/bonus payouts in a couple of years, at most. 7. IBM no longer considers technology it's key offering after Global Technology Sevices GTS vertical of IBM, became a seperate legal entity now known as KYNDRYL, as IBM gradually shifts to the consulting domain as mentioned earlier. 8. "Blind leading the blind", for the lack of a better phrase, is the most common scenario on top of the above points w.r.t. BAU trainings. Add to this the fact that almost every individual contributor is often cut off from their peers w.r.t. profesional collaboration, by design. There are, however, mandatory trainings assigned to everyone in the learning portal that are often redundant in terms if information or are irrelevant entirely. 9. To end on a lighter note while simultaneously highlighting an irony  No member of the HR team in IBM, can be reached out to for having a direct conversation face to face, instant messengers, and/or emails. There is an automated HR bot and a common mail box that conveniently separates the the "Human Resources" team from the other humans hired by the firm :D so may be join HR team for retirement?  Please note: Feedback points stated are based on my subjective experience in working with IBM and may vary significantly from other IBMers. Pros: IBM has/had an excellent software product line, with both bredth and depth.  IBM also has some outstanding technical, sales, development and marketing people. However, the effectiveness "Team IBM" is often diluted by the product pillar mentality:  our executive focus on a particular product pillar, rather than the overall solution that the customer buys.  While we talk a great solutions game, it is still painful to implement.  There is a lot to be learned at IBM, but I'd suggest you not consider it your end job  think about where you want this company, and your role in it, to take you!
Cons: This company once had a culture based on quality, customer satisfaction, and respect for the individual.  These are no longer values held by our executives.  Commitments  made to business partners, clients, and employees  are not kept.  Executives are not held accountable:  the employees are.  The executives are given a quota for "management initiated separations" and despite an employee's track record and prior performance, an employee may be dropped from a 1 to a 3 and immediately place on the "measured mile".  Even though this runs counter our published guidelines!   An "Open Door" will only back the executive, regardless of the evidence.  This had not been the case in the past!.  On top of this, routine "downsizings" cull the herd, regardless of performance rating.  The employment relationship at IBM is out of balance:  IBM holds all the cards.  Few people get beyond 5 years of service anymore. While some of this may be due to globalization, and some of this is not avoidable, most of it comes from the view by IBM executive leadership that people are no longer desirable resources, but only an expense to be controlled.  They're missing the point that a loyal employee will produce so much more than one just doing his time.  Presently, IBM is schizophrenic:  there are some outstanding people in IBM who live up to the old expectations and basic beliefs, and others who are just collecting their unearned executive bonuses.

Pros: I have very mixed feelings about this company. Joined during the IT boom in the late '90s and worked in many roles such as developer, dev lead, project manager, product and solutions architect, lead architect, presales and client architect. There is a lot I have to thank the people who _worked there_ for, the people on the ground, developing the company's products and solutions as well as a handful of people in other roles. When I joined, Lou Gerstner had just turned this sinking super tanker around, and more or less saved IBM, so the atmosphere was very positive, cash flow was great, props were fantastic similar to startups today and one could pretty much pick and choose to do whatever one wanted to do. At that time the company supported explorers and out of the box thinkers, both monetarily and with strong encouragement from the management layers. If you did a good job, successful projects or create some program even internal ones that solved real business problems saved / earned money, you were rewarded with rich cash awards and/or stock. It was a very attractive place, with high concentration of talent.
Cons: The golden era ended shortly after the IT bubble burst. Sam Palmisano had taken over and instead of just steering the tanker straight ahead in the direction Gerstner had left it in, Sam decided that gutting the company and punching holes in the hull would be a better strategy. About 2005 most employees globally could feel their feet had become wet with murky water.   The outsourcing trend started to wash over the western world in earnest, organic talent recruitment to IBM was replaced by mostly strategically noncomplementary company acquisitions. Jobs mostly in the US were shipped to offshore centers, primarily to India. Price Waterhouse Coopers Consulting's "IT department" was bought, and outsourcing started dominating the entire IBM culture. Outsourcing IBM jobs as well as jobs of its customers the PWCC influence changed _that_ term to "clients", as IBM mistakenly thought it was PWC for a while. This was the start of the cancer that still continues to eat IBM from the inside.  The problem I have with IBM is what I experienced since 2005, a straight line to the sea bottom, with a bridge crew that has no idea whatsoever about navigation, innovation, technology nor how you can make money from it. Stark contrast to how it started out.  Short summary of events since then, to give the reader some context to why IBM is where it is, and to help visualize the trajectory this company has had for the last decade. 1. Strategy is cost cutting: trim the fat. 2. Strategy is cost cutting: Sell business units, printers, networking, desktops. 3. Strategy is cost cutting: Trim all the perks, attractive employer status be damned! 4. Strategy is cost cutting: Halt and then cancel bonuses, freeze salary increases, except for upper mgmt. 5. Strategy is cost cutting: Trim the muscles, mass exodus of the real talent. 6. Tactic for a one time stock value boost: Sell the laptop division. 7. Strategy is cost cutting: Sell further business, servers, chip fabs and R&D capabilities. 8. Strategy is cost cutting: Trim the bones as well, force out the fan club / "lifers" as well.  Ginni the current CEO of the company was handed a sinking ship, so I gave her a benefit of a doubt, waited little over a year for her to get her footing, and when she finally emerged from her cave, it was unfortunately the exact same Palmisano playbook. That broke my heart, and made me lose all faith in IBM, as it was then clear IBM had no future.  From what I've heard since, from the few former colleagues still clinging to the husk of what used to be IBM, it's still the same aimless floundering with brand reorgs, org. reorgs and disconnected speak, same as the day I left.  For anyone thinking about joining IBM, please think hard. They'll paint a rosey picture they're still good with lofty words, but don't take the words at face value.  If you are talented and want to grow as an individual or in your technical field, put this company at the bottom of your stack of places you consider seeking employment. If all other options fail to pan out, then you have this left, and they're pretty much taking anyone today in certain departments. Negotiate hard to compensate for you not going to receive a raise later on. View the employment as a contract work where the contract can be cancelled at any moment, as loyalty and "IBM family" notions died mid 2000. And be prepared to work hard. They still employ the Vitality Curve google it!, also known as the cooperative culture Poison. ___________________________________________________________ Disclaimer: This review reflects my own experience at the company up until 2014. I have no first hand knowledge of what has transpired at the company since. The review is based on what I perceived and is naturally a subjective piece in it's entirety.

Pros:
I decided to wait almost a year after leaving the company before posting a review.  The primary reason being is that when you decide to leave an organization it is usually because there is something there that isn't aligning with you or what you want anymore however, the grass is not always greener someplace else.  This has been my experience.  In fact, the appreciation I have for the company has grown so much in my time away that I would really like to return.

The company truly believes on promoting within and as an employee you are encouraged to grow your career within the organization and learn new skills by taking different positions.  Benefits are excellent.  Cisco is the industry leader for networking and now cloud.  It is sometimes easy to forget that on the daily grind but you are working for the company that everyone looks to for network and infrastructure standards.  Culture within the business units managing product lines give you a lot of freedom to be innovative and creative in your approach to your role.  In most cases you are given a fair amount of autonomy and control over how you do your job provided that it aligns with the strategic objectives.  Benefits, 401k match, RSUs and ESPP are amazing.  And while the salaries aren't the top of the industry, they are above market and pretty competitive.
Cons:
Cisco can be a machine.  There isn't an overt demand for all of your time even the time outside of work but more of a subtle, slight encouragement to always be on.  If you are not careful, you will live, sleep and eat Cisco 24x7.  Don't get me wrong, this is 100% a choice and if you are aware of this subtlety in the culture it is very easy to set appropriate boundaries that will be respected by the company and leadership team.

If you don't like where you are in Cisco or what you are working on, give it 6 months because you will be reorg'd.  While it is sometimes necessary to realign the company to meet competitive threats or market demands, reorganizing the company once a year is excessive and tends to create a distrusting environment for the rank and file which makes being a leader in the organize challenging.  There is a loss of momentum and motivation that occurs a few months before and a few months after reorgs so this leaves the company being effective at delivery and execution only about 70% of the time.

While Cisco attracts some bright, motivated people the truth of the matter is you are either cut out for the company and its culture or you're not.  If you aren't it will be painfully obvious to you and those around you.  Sadly as a leader it is hard to cut dead weight from the team and the only really accepted way is via layoffs, which is why the company reorgs once a year despite the company line about the reorgs.

Pros: Overall, Cisco is a good place to work. As a senior systems engineer, I had the opportunity to collaborate with many thoughtful, capable, and genuine people across teams—from engineering and test to compliance, product management, executives, manufacturing, and TAC. The company encourages technical excellence, and there are pockets of genuinely supportive leadership. That said, the experience can vary dramatically depending on your org and manager, and some managers operate with impunity despite repeated and serious concerns.
Cons:
If you end up with a manager who manipulates systems and relationships—undermining direct reports, peers, and even superiors to secure promotion or survival—the only real option is to leave. Don’t expect HR, ER, or internal processes to intervene meaningfully, even when misconduct is extensively documented and corroborated by multiple witnesses. This toxic behavior often goes unpunished and actively rewarded—with visibility, advancement, incentives, and plenty of opportunities to retaliate against those who speak up.

Cisco has trimmed HR/ER and internal enforcement functions so much that the cultural messaging from the Cisco People Office feels performative and aspirational rather than reflective of groundlevel realities.

For instance, the “top performer” in my group was actually absent on vacation for a large part of the timeline, and despite multiple complaints about their performance, program management ignored these concerns and selected that person as the only one from our group to receive LIFT honors.

The current class is regarded as having a poor attitude, often logging in after 11 a.m. and frequently complaining. 

Overall, if you're one of Tim’s favorites, you may have a smoother path, but if not, expect to face politics rather than professional growth. The LIFT Program needs strong, unbiased leadership to restore its reputation and value.

Once Cisco came in to take over in the last year, they stopped listening to the advice of most tenured team members within AppD who knew the AppD business best. I worked for almost 6 years before moving to different company.  The policies are employee friendly, good campus  BangaloreCessna park, good cafeteria, company provided transportation is the best, up to $100 per month internet bill reimbursement, easy to change teams internally. 
HR team and policies are women friendly.
Cons:
# Too many Org. changes, frequent layoffs, stupid 1st line managers who have no clue how to manage senior resources. 
# Hikes are unpredictable  sometimes two consecutive cycles are missed, sometimes the numbers are really low. 
# Getting promotion is next to impossible if you are a G8/above.  You need to be a really good bootlicker to get consistent hikes/promotion. 
Annual performance review is a joke manager rates you as he wishes rarely based upon your performance
# New College grads are being hired at salary higher than people working in cisco with 68 years of workexp. 
# Some 1st/2nd line managers behave as if they are the CEO of the company arrogant and unprofessional attitude.
# Lack of strategic vision for future by the top management. 
# NOT a company to stay for more than a few years you constantly have the layoff sword hanging over your head!!!

Pros:
Excellent talent.  The people you work with are the best in the business.
 The benefits are very good.
 You are always challenged.
 There is always something to learn.
Cons:
Salaries are low for the industry...there is a feeling that you should accept this because you work at Cisco.
 It is very hard to get promoted, or get raises.  Senior management routinely will stop all raises for years at a time, meaning that the only way to get a raise is by an "equity adjustment".
 Teamwork is poor, when you send an email or leave a voicemail, the first thing most people do is look you up in the directory to see your title, if it is not good enough, don't plan on hearing anything back from that person.

Pros:
Cisco's People Deal is real and is pervasive in all of the moments that matter in your career. From your recruitment through retirement/moving on, Cisco aims to make sure they make each "Moment that Matters" special.

The HR Leadership Program HRLP has given me multiple rotations through various HR specialties, giving me a good base knowledge of HR and has helped me identify where my strengths and passion will allow me to contribute at a high level.

In HR you are treated like a true professional. As long as you're performing at an acceptable level, no one pays attention to or cares where, when, and how you get your work done.  This is great for work flexibility. I have worked from several locations for extended periods of time only needing to take part of that time as Paid Time Off, and not missed a beat.

The technology plays a large role in the work flexibility as in any given day I can be talking with people from any part of the world, facetoface over WebEx or Telepresence video.
Cons: As the technology can allow for great work flexibility, it can also allow work  if you don't proactively manage it  to take over your life as you CAN always be available.  Manage your schedule with your stakeholders and you'll be fine.

Pros: Love it here great work
Cons: Always on your feet gets tiring

Pros: At all levels of the organization, there is emphasis and value put on diversity in the workplace.  Many leaders understand the beauty and strength of our differences, and are not interested in creating a cookie cutter employee.  Many of the perks of being a Cisco employee highlight how much they want to take care of their employees, such as the onsite health and fitness centers, family events on campus, etc, but they go beyond these "nice to have" items and back up their words in the work.  My opinion is appreciated most when it differs from those around me and offers a fresh perspective.  We also have very strong communities to support each other and enable success of the individual.
Cons: There are very few cons when it comes to working for Cisco.  It certainly isn't like a startup environment and ideas can take longer to put into action because of the bureaucracy that comes with a company of over 70k employees, but you can learn to navigate these waters smoothly.  There is vibrancy and learning at Cisco that you won't find elsewhere.

Pros: Despite my initial reservations and shynesss I have grown more confident as a gay employee at Cisco as Cisco’s leadership and its policies towards the LGBT community have grown to be more progressive. It took one call to HR and zero paperwork to add my partner to benefits. When I reached our  HR to say I had come out and wanted to know if there was an employee group, their first words were “congratulations.” Our resell partners sponsor an LGBT social at our annual sales conference we have the best resell partners on the planet. And we have executive sponsors who honestly care about our welfare. They matched my donations to Orlando, PRIDE, and supported us in the San Francisco parade. They are sensitive to the situations other employees face in other countries.
Cons: They are not leaders; rather, fast followers in LGBT advocacy. In North Carolina. In Texas. In Washington. At the San Fran parade. Room to grow. Not a place to expect leadership. But a place to expect acceptance, decency and support.

Pros: Eh nothing much but food
Cons: Crappy management and need better pay

Pros: Flexible work environment though varies significantly with the manager, good benefits. Easy to do minimal work and stay employed for many years.
Cons:
Little chance for advancement, many vicious selfpromoting middle management who lead with fear. HR is useless of course, and upper mgmt is too stupid to see what's going on. Last many years have gone way over board hiring undergrads who many of which have contributed nothing after 23 years. I know a few who are great, but most get by on being cute and perky, while the long term employees are forced to cover. 

Annual layoffs mostly hit those who do the most work, while middle management stays fat. Reorgs are done on a regular basis just because. If the current structure was so great last year why have yet another reorg?

I've been moved 10 times between teams often even my own manager didn't know about it. No one asks if you want to move to that team, or if your skills are what is needed. We're just numbers.

Pros: culture, benefits, flexibility, pay, opportunity
Cons: big company, slow moving, corporate,

Pros:
Impactual Work
Mid level management and lower level people are really great to work with
Great Flexibility. You can definitely work at any time
No fourloughs!!
Cons:
It's not a democracy, so never ever think for a second it is. It is a command control system, so don't let them fool you by saying it is not. When the decisions come from the top, very little input comes from those on the bottom
Cisco is somewhat too much of a fiscal conserative company. In this environment, it is a good thing, but everything has a line, and they seem to have crossed that line. They seem to overpay for acquisitions and not invest enough in the employees they currently have. They always say they want to be the leader or benchmark, but when you need funding for a project, or cuts in discretionary spending happen, they state that they are just following industry standard.. somewhat ironic. 
Career advacement is too much determined on who you know, than what you do.

Pros: Cisco has excellent benefits for regular employees, including all the health, vision, dental, 401k, ESPP, family bonding leave, and other benefits that are part of big company compensation in Silicon Valley.  Cisco has a good internal training and learning site that gives you access to many resources for improving your knowledge. The culture is modern and socially liberal, embracing diversity is encouraged.  And, if you are laid off, the severance package is generous.
Cons: I was part of an acquisition at Cisco.  And while it was handled well, and the transition went pretty smoothly, after a few years Cisco gutted our business in one of it's perennial layoffs. It was a disappointment, since we were making money and doing well compared to other acquisitions.  You cannot allow yourself to forget that Cisco is a big company, and if you are not working on something that's making a great deal of money there, Cisco is not likely to understand your business well enough to grow it.

Pros: Large company, good benefit, good environment, people are extremely nice to each other.  A very nice view of Great America and Silicon Valley from the building.  A very diverse company.
Cons: This is for WebEx, a company Cisco bought about a year ago.  This has nothing to do with Cisco, but WebEx alone.  Basically, whoever speaks the loudest will get recognized, not the person who gets the most done.   So hard work and talents usually do not get rewarded with recognition or compensation.  Many valuable talents have left the company because of beauracracy and politics. There are too many midlevel managers that worry about their job security too much, and discourage employee growth.   It is a stable place to be in terms of job security, but if you are young and want to learn and advance, this is not a good place for you.

Pros: Friendly employees, great culture, lots of good benefits and new products coming out.  The San Jose campus is massive, with just over 50 buildings, and there is always work going on somewhere.  The work environment is also good, and the labs are generally well organized.  They also have free soda/tea/coffee, and you can occasionally find free food by going to various presentations.  There are also two gyms and a daycare center, and provide great benefits to fulltime employees.  I accumulated the equivalent of 3.5 weeks PTO per year as a coop/intern, the same as any regular employee.
Cons: There are too many managers and executives, and endless business/technical meetings which do not contribute much in fact the most useful meetings are the meet&greet because they encourage teamwork, even though they have nothing to do with your job.  Also, the work can be slow and boring at times, and you will not be immune to "burnout" at Cisco.  As a coop, I received no benefits other than PTO and hourly pay.

Pros: Cisco remains a challenging environment, driven for excellence. For those able to keep up, you're rewarded well, and surrounded by expert peers, managers, and senior managers committed to your success. Training, lab equipment, peer support are readily available for any assignment or task. The mutual respect and support make Cisco a wonderful place to work. The good pay and excellent benefits add icing to the cake. Working from home is a huge plus! The customers are also very easy to work with because they recognize and respect the level of expertise Cisco engineers bring to the conversation. I love my customers!
Cons: The demand for your expertise is constant. You have to know how to delegate responsibility to other teams, and learn how to use your resources, the sales team, and partners to get the job done. Otherwise, you'll end up working 12 hour days constantly. My colleagues who don't delegate are probably accusing me of only working half a day!

Pros:
There is always something new to learn and keep things interesting
 There are plenty of opportunities to move within the company
 Truly care about the individual especially during difficult personal times. And I've seen time and again Senior Execs step in and help.
 Great benefits especially Medical for my and my families needs
 full week of community service beyond your PTO and everyone is encouraged to find someway to give back
 strong Senior Exec leadership especially during tough times
Cons:
During annual 'Limited Restructures', it's not about being a rock star or not, it's your position that is eliminated including whole teams
 Tight weekly commits can cause stress within teams depending on management
 Marketing has continued to overpromise or oversell, Cisco didn't use to sell on roadmaps
 dilution of culture. when I first started you could call anyone from John Chambers down and you would get a response. Now, it's not uncommon for someone to not respond unless you cc: their manager and yours.

Pros:
Decent Pay
Good 401k match at 4.5%, vests 100% upon match
Some of the best products for collaboration, data center
Flex time and telecommuting is the norm
Cons:
Cisco continues to cut jobs through massive layoffs 5500 direct and another 8500 through early retirement. Some were double CCIE's and many were CCIE's. This does not show value in employee skills 
No strategy for IoT
Executive Management does a poor job communicating strategy
Internal transfers are difficult
Services margins are too high to build an IoT line of business
Syncups has replaced a poor personnel performance ranking system, but few managers follow,the policy on conducting the sync ups.

Pros: Collaborative work environment. Everyone loves what they do and as a result, they work as a cohesive unit. Great leadership, not too much of a heirarchy. If you have a good idea, then you can take it to the top. Very responsible socially too. A lot of community service opportunities and they definitely care about others. This is not any other greedy corporation. It's a wonderful place where you can grow and develop rapport with fellow employees. I loved my time there and I hope that you will consider it to be one of your top choices as well. Good luck!
Cons: I really don't think there's anything wrong with Cisco. I'd say the only probably is that it is so large, that it is hard to find your way around the company. But that's the case with any other company of this size as well. I would suggest that they strengthen their internal communications, otherwise things will get lost in translation. They're also placing a great emphasis on the future, but if these projections turn out to be remarkably inaccurate, this could be very detrimental to the company and your long term future. So theres' a risk involved, as is the case with most tech companies

Job Title: Low Level Engineer Doing The Work
Pros:
Good pay and benefits. 
Can be interesting work in the write department. 
Top level and bottom level workers are good at what they do.
If you have good social skills and want to climb up the ladder then there are good opportunities if your face fits.
Cons:
Lower management is a joke and more like a boys club. 
Priorities are themselves, then the project then if there is any time/energy left their staff.
They lack of knowledge on how to handle exceptional engineers/people, the ones who come with side effects, so good is the best they will get/keep.
The top people at the bottom i.e. the engineers doing the work often do not have great social skills and management can't handle them no matter how good they are at their job of for the project..
You have to spend more time looking after your career than doing the job if you want to climb, it's not a place to survive at the bottom level for long. If you want to stay hand's on then Cisco isn't for you no matter how good you are.

Pros: There are some wonderful employees at Cisco, and generally a very strong work ethic.  Most people are genuinely trying to do their best for the company.  There is a good opportunity to work globally and certainly to experience interaction with people from around the world, using virtual collaboration tools.
Cons: Weak HR means that managers deal with an antiquated performance management process based on a 15 year old GE model; lots of unhealthy politics at the SVP level and too many Directors sitting pretty due to tenure; recent RIFs have taken a slice out of the workforce, but not out of the much more expensive layers of the organisation.

Pros:
Cisco has the perfect balance of innovation, from a technical perspective, and established business practices with a strong customer base. A primary benefit to employees is a reasonable pace. It's possible to do excellent work without sacrificing one's personal goals and the work environment is definitely more collaborative than competitive. An additional benefit is the ability to move about the company to work on different products and projects. 
The employee population is remarkably diverse and both the executive leadership and HR underscore the value of inclusion and collaboration diversity in both it's composition and everything it says and does. Cisco takes diversity very, very seriously.
Deep support for working remotely is absolutely outstanding! We're able to draw  talent from all over the world instead of limiting ourselves to only those people who are willing to live in or near Silicon Valley.
Cons: The overall culture isn't quite as tech intensive as the culture I've experienced at major software  and services companies such as Microsoft.  At other companies for example, demos of products in development were a critical component of any meeting. At Cisco we tend to focus on the bigger business picture.

Pros:
Great Benefits
High Pay
Work from home
Friendly People
Cons:
Lack of control over anything that you do. "Architect" teams in the marketing department make all decisions and promises without consulting the engineers. Due to management structure, these decisions cannot be appealed.

As an intern, I was put on a team that was in no way prepared to take on an intern. They had great difficulty giving me anything to do. The one real project I had took me 3 weeks, after that, despite asking for more work I was barely given anything to do.

My entire team was very upset with management and the decisions being made, but was powerless to even voice these opinions.

Satellite locations get overlooked a lot. You are a second class employee if you're anywhere but San Jose.

I saw multiple instances of people being hired as developers and then being placed into a sysadmin job under the guise of devopts.

Oh yeah, and they're laying off 20% of their workforce.

Pros:
Just brand name, legacy reputation, and big market capture in Networking domain. 
 It's a group of many small startups, say. So, if you fall in good BU, you will get good work, exposure, hikes, and live in peace.
 Nice clean big campus, facilities, gym, office infra.
 Pays huge to freshers from premium colleges, and to Senior Management.
Cons:
Pays Low Salary as per market standard of Product companies. Lesser than some big service companies.  Always postpone yearly hike cycles by 1 or 2 quarters.
 Regular firing/LR.
 Too much work pressure. Too many product lines make it difficult to learn for Engineers. Customer escalations, bug counts are day to day worries. Very few old employees left who know product details, so no one is there to help.  
 Managers & Sr. Managers insulate engineers from Directors & VP who are real decision makers for hike & promotions. So midlevel engineers suffer from both side lot of difficult work, and minimal hikes. Managers take credit & themselves get promoted.
 More suffering for people in Infra, platform, services, etc.

Pros:
1. I experienced the most comprehensive training as a graduate. Before joined in Cisco, I know nothing about network and data center. Cisco invested on all CSAP to receive the best training in IT industry.

2. Work culture here is very openminded. You can have happy hour with your manager and chat with your seniors. Any feedback is welcome in cisco. 

3. mentorship is a good culture in Cisco. My mentors are experienced sales. Besides the training content, my mentors' words are also important to me. Mentors' experience is the best local sales case study.

4. The whole CSAPers is a big family. you will have chance to know your colleagues from all over the world. I experience the family union culture in cisco. This is very very vital for young people especially for someone likes to social networking.
Cons: I work in APJC area, personally speaking, the business model is different from America. What you have learned in CSAP training will be probably a little different than the real world. But keep learning, don't settle!

Pros:
Good people majority of my managers and employees have been smart and self motivated.  People care about their jobs, care about their coworkers, care about the community.

Love the moto:  "Best in the world, Best for the world".    Relentless focus on execution, without losing need to do good in the world.  

Great worklife balance.  Employees work hard, but flex time is the norm.  Very common to have 7am calls, 7pm calls, but also ok to be coaching soccer at 4pm, or at doctor's appt with your mother in the middle of the day
Cons:
Many people have been here a long time there's a sense of entitlement amongst those here 20+ years.  Some complacency, related to above.

Hard to move up promotions to director level and above seems to require inside connections.

Pros:
Extremely flexible employment, also means you are expected to work anytime, everytime. Still, being able to work from home, from a cafeteria, or from another country's Cisco office is great.
A lot depends on who your direct manager is, whether they support and promote you or aim to exploit and ditch you once you got burned out. Dynamic environment. Ability to work with the newest gadgets. Some nice people, some .ssh..es, as everywhere.
Cons: Work is nonstop, no time off  they call it worklife balance, but this is actually working all the time. You are the coolest if you join videoconference meetings from your annual holiday on an island. Actually happens. Pay is relatively OK so most people tend to work as hard as they can while the income lasts, as you can never be sure whether the next reorg will get away with you.

Pros: Cisco pays pretty well and offers good flexibility and some perks, and some of the administrative things work surprisingly well for such a giant corporation.  Cisco does a lot of good work in the community and encourages staff to give back to various charities, etc. and does a good job of promoting mobility across job functions, etc.
Cons: There is a constant threat of a "Limited Restructuring"  nearly every year, you will lose some colleagues if not your own job, which absolutely kills morale.  They make a lot of noise about how great their culture is  which if you have to say it so often, means it is likely not the case.  They can be completely tonedeaf, for example, scheduling allhands, AMAtype townhall meetings with execs on the same days they're laying off hundreds of people, making "The People Deal" complete BS.

Pros: Work from home, competitive pay, market leader in everything
Cons: Too many all hands calls to bash white people and scream racism. In your face die hard liberal leadership. Gave $1M to BLM. CEO recently said we don't want your thoughts and prayers they don't work anymore. We need to take action. This in regards to recent violence in the US. Desperately anti gun. Blindly follows anything Liberal politicians tell them to with no regard to other views. Publicly bashed white people, Republicans, pro 2nd amendment employees, and likened them all to terrorists and racists!

Pros: Lots of really smart people with good salaries and benefits. Cisco is still light years ahead of a lot of companies and that allows you to be able to move to other companies fairly easily after you've workes at Cisco. Also, being able to move around within the company used be a lot easier to do, but the last few years has been really locked down.
Cons: Marketing Operations specifically Management is terrible and one director in particular is completely unprofessional and has burned out a number of high quality employees. The result is a huge turn over rate in Operations and in Marketing as well. The senior management seems to allow it to continue. The result is a very negative environment with no career growth.

Pros: This is a big company with a lot of great employees and a lot of innovation.  Cisco does not want to join the long list of previously great Silicon Valley companies that missed a market transition.  They are constantly trying new strategies which gets a little exhausting at times, throwing stuff at the wall and seeing what sticks.  I think the salary, bonus, and RSUs for top performers are very strong.
Cons: 20052014 I thought Cisco was a great place to work, but not a good stock to own.  Now it is kind of the opposite.  If your Business Unit is not growing by 10% annually, you will get your budget cut proportionally and that money will go to the growing BUs.  Our BU growth slowed, and we got cut a little in 2014, a LOT in 2016, and now again in 2017 including me.

Pros: Great company. Great work culture. Highly talented people. The company provides opportunities for growth, career transitions, mentoring. I mean it's up to the employee to make the best use of the opportunities available. I got my immigration work also done by Cisco. Even after I left Cisco, I got support from Fragomen. I must say I am very very impressed by the way Cisco takes care of their employees and former employees.
Cons: I don't like the new open workspace concept. It's very chaotic and highly unproductive. Most of the employees at Cisco don't like it. I didn't meet anyone who liked it. But still, it was enforced. It was disappointing to see Cisco didn't care about employees opinion. I can understand that it's highly costeffective to stuff double the employees in the same old space.

Pros:
I learned a tremendous amount during my time with Cisco
 Benefits are pretty good, better than most other companies in my geographic area
