Pros: Cisco has historically been a great place to work. Management does care about the employees and their personal well being. The work is challenging and can be satisfying and rewarding. More recently with the troubles in Cisco's business the company is changing for the worse. There has been massive attrition of key engineers and engineering leaders and Cisco doesn't seem to be able to stop this trend. While the company is certainly not a disaster and the problems it faces are recoverable it needs to move quickly and decisively which is something it has not been able to do for the past 3+ years since it implemented the boards and councils management structure a mistake John Chambers is directly responsible for. Since then most of this structure has been removed and now its about getting the right leaders in place. Compensation is relatively fair especially if you have a good manager who recognizes who the contributors are. Benefits are really good to...
Cons: Attrition is a major issue right now and Cisco needs to stop the bleeding quickly and figure out not only how its going to retain the top talent but attract new talent which is especially difficult in Silicon Valley where there are many startups wooing the top talent as well as employees leaving to join the red hot social networking companies. You need talented engineers to build the best products and solutions in the market and while this won't effect the company in the next 12  18 months you will see the impact outside of that. The executive team is a group of extremely bright and talented business people but that is also the biggest problem is that there are no true Engineers at the top of the company and this is a technology company who needs great executive technology leadership!

Pros: Great people. Good community. Great use of own technology to enable collaboration and anywhere, anytime, any device connectivity. Home office setup was great!
Cons: A little too big and too redundant in some areas, causing duplicate efforts or unnecessary waiting for resolution of conflicts. Working to resolve, at least on operations side.

Pros: Lots of people with families and CEO John Chambers fosters a familyatmosphere. While you can put in lots of hours, stress levels are kept pretty low. We get the job done, but we don't' run over people to do it. Great benefits including the company medical facility in San Jose and employee Gym. Very smart people here and it's bay area. Traditionally a strong rotation culture but see cons list on this one. Generous bonuses. You also get a frontrow seat on some pretty awesome technology and vision for the future.
Cons:
Cisco does a terrible job identifying talent and promoting them, as a result of this and the recent layoffs and market challenges, I think Cisco is seeing a bit of a brain drain. I know and hear of plenty of notable talent heading for the doors. one reason they're leaving is this company prefers outside talent to fill open positions which clogs the top and greatly limits upward mobility. While traditionally a rotation company, which is great, open reqs have been almost all shut down coupled with the new focus of hiring in RTP North Carolina complicates and limits available rotations in San Jose. 
There's also very limited equity adjustments and a weak mechanism for distribution. After several years I learned new hires at my same level were being offered salaries higher than my own. That tells me Cisco values my time here less than brand new people and is the completely wrong message. Another gentle push out the door.

Pros:
Great salary when compared against other companies' internship programs.

If you're working at the San Jose campus, you'll find many other college students scattered across the campus, as Cisco hires students from a variety of universities across the country. As other reviews have mentioned, the new hire program offers opportunities to meet with your peers.

You will be working on pertinent projects with fulltime employees, doing the same [if not similar] things they're doing. If your team is busy, you'll be busy too.

There's an "opendoor" culture at work  if you have questions or concerns, you are free to bring it up to your manager or coworkers. Many of them are more than willing to help you learn and contribute while you're here.
Cons:
If you're not a local, relocating to San Jose can be confusing. Although Cisco offers relocation compensation, it'll be up to you to find a place to live for the next 3 to 6 months. "Corporate housing" is not offered for interns and coops. However, the Silicon Valley area has seen so many interns/temps that many neighborhoods/apartments offer shortterm or monthtomonth leases.

This might not seem like a "con" especially if you're a college student, but if your team needs you to stay until midnight to get something done, expect to do so and expect overtime pay as well.

Despite my short stay, I have definitely caught a whiff of the stagnating bureaucracy that can drive you, your project, and your coworkers nuts. But I suppose this is what happens in a "big company."

Pros: Large company, many products, lots of opportunities and innovation. You could easily spend a lifetime at Cisco and never run out of challenges.

Financially sound with diverse portfolio of products and services, able to endure tough times better than many other companies

Engineers are viewed and treated as a commodity, not as the engine of product development.

Career growth is nonexistent.  There is no benefit to moving within the company because you can't get a promotion or raise even if you get hired for a position that is a higher grade level.

Your direct manager has no say in your evaluation rating, it is all rolled up to executive levels who arbitrarily rank order you.

Cisco loves to talk about hiring the top 5% of talent, then they want to compensate them at the 70th percentile if that, and not recognize their efforts.  This causes low morale and limits the effort that people are willing to put into their work. Cisco wants you to be "happy you still have a job" in the current environment and they manage by fear.  Apple employees are asked to work like it is a startup, but they still get broad based stock grants.

Pros: I just passed my 10 year anniversary and am still proud to work at Cisco. The benefits are varied and quite good, lots of vacation earned 6.16 hrs / pay period and caps at 280 hours. Lots of nonmonetary rewards like gymnasium, child care, dry cleaning, car wash, new medical facility, free soda and water although not for long, and telecommuting options although this varies greatly by group and manager, the pay for my monthly home broadband too $62/month. Lots of online education and the tuition reimbursement is great $7500/year. Fortunately I work in a fairly decent group marketing with minimal politics except for a few highly volitle people. I have an engineering background so like the mix of business and technical. If you're a technical person, it's a pretty good gig.
Cons:
I don't know where the many people who wrote reviews here work who said there is good work/life balance because I've never seen it. I have never worked less than 55 hrs/week and often 80+ hrs.  There absolutely are duds here who are great at talking nonstop and so get recognized but they don't do anything. I get frustrated working at a high tech company and constantly get asked stupid questions about how to use Excel or PowerPoint or things they can easily look up themselves. How can someone get a job here and not know computer basics is beyond me. Just because they're busy doesn't mean they're productive basic computer skills would be a great improvement.

I also don't like the performance review system which many others mentioned. It's an absolute joke and not a good one. Your score has little to do with the quality of your work, but how much your manager likes you, how much work s/he is willing to do to help you get ahead, and how lazy they are. I've had managers tell me they never give an X the highest score no matter what you do and everyone gets the same rating because it's easier for the manager. I was fortunate to finally get a promotion last year and two raises but it was a horrific, buttkissing process. I've had over 15 CAP awards over the years but none of that seems to matter. You can do the exact same work for manager A and get a E score but then move to manager B and get an X, it makes no sense and there is no oversight or standards.

Pros: This role allows one to run their own book of business. Though the technology is complex in nature, but there are many learning resources. My team is super helpful. Pros: Relaxed environment, people are great and it is enjoyable. Cisco make great use of the technology they have WebEx, telepresence etc which makes working with global colleagues a breeze.

Pros: Work with smart, engaged people in a collaborative environment.  The company has the power to shape markets, and has clout when working with customers and partners.
Cons: Always working...no downtime.  It is expected that you are available/accessible at all times, including nights and weekends.  Downsizing has only increased the pressure on those that remain.  There is still too much bureaucracy.

Pros: Company cares about the environment and promotes a fun work place.  There is somewhat a flexible schedule and they promote rotation.
Cons: There is no stability , for the past 4 years the company has laid off many employees and then they open new jobs and does not give the opportunity to these employees to find a job in the area of growth.  Individual contributors do not feel like they can be heard, and when they are, they are usually the ones that are let go.  Company promotes rotation, but it makes it very hard for an employee to rotate .  They have no clear paths to promotion.  There is no life work balance as the hours are long and hectic, although some departments allow employees to work remotely.  The company advertises that there is tuition reimbursement for a career that aligns with the company as a whole, but they fail to let the employee know that if you are rotating to a new department, that department does not have to honor your tuition reimbursement leaving employees with the financial burden or an incomplete degree.   Accounting and Finance culture reminds me of a high school clique , and not everyone is accepted in the circle.

Pros: Some great people with a passion to succeed
Cons: Extremely poor leadership, lack of focus and clear objectives creates an atmosphere of internal competition and jockeying for position. Leftover culture that operates out of fear leads to many talented people either leaving or just putting their head down and doing bare minimum.

Pros: Good environment to learn different processes, technology and how to work and survive in enterprise environment which runs in different paces depending on which group and project you are on, nice people who are mostly willing to help, teach and collaborate.
Cons: Just like any large companies, sometimes there are too much red tapes and processes that impede the project execution.  Other that, overall good company to work for.

Pros: Cisco is an established company who knows what they're doing.  They are serious about their image as a family oriented company.  It really feels like you are part of a community, although I'm sure that view changes wildly based on your team.
Cons: They are a large corporation, with a large and strange bureaucracy at times.  Everything moves slowly and requires quite a bit of fighting to get pushed through.

Pros: Opportunity to work and contribute directly with industry idea / product leaders. Strong in place processes and methods for product management. Opportunity to affect very large scale sales base with exceptionally talented field sales/support teammates. A wide variety of offerings may provide some lateral opportunities.  Decent to better total compensation.  Executive management espouses and somewhat really means the high culture and values.
Cons: Many visions and agendas that can openly conflict are not only tolerated but appear to be accepted by management. While in the past this could lead to good idea competition that could result in multiple winners, it's now become much more one side "We are the only smart, capable team, you are not us, so don't ever think you can" and other side "We must keep going and understand that other investments must be made...oh and ignore that you are often reminded that you are lessthans and treated that way".   Unfortunately this has significantly dropped the professionalism of the organization.  Last, the culture has also shifted strongly to a  high reward for the top few, low reward for the remainder, and removal of any who are not in synch at that time.  This is at odds with the culture and values espoused. The result has been a significant tide of midtohigh experience staff turn over 815+ year staff for which so many reasons management stated, but first hand knowledge from those staff says they just didn't want to deal with this any longer.

Pros:
Great benefits for employees outside Silicon Valley. Respectable benefits for Silicon Valley Companies.
Generally higher than average local salaries than other companies in RTP.
Many opportunities to learn and grow professionally, so long as you drive your growth.
Topnotch people to work with in US.
Complex technology.
Cisco culture. IC's allowed to make deisions
PTO at 4 wks starting can't be beat.

Cisco is very risk adverse for long term projects. Some are ahead of their time, but company not willing to develop market or save product for when market is available.
New products only seem to build on existing. Market share loss to cloud vendors, etc. New Security services along with Advanced Sere vices pulling in most of money
Work loads can vary by groups.  Yearly layoffs becoming a thing.  Seems that it's quicker and less expensive to lay off top technical people and hire new ones with some new expertise, rather that really invest in and develop current dedicated staff.
Mobile worker cubes and open work environments not conducive to burying your head into work.
I'm sure there are far worse places to work in North Carolina

Pros: Probably one of the few very good places to work. truely innovative and flexible, great plans, strategy, people and modern.

Pros:
This is a great sales training rotational program for people with sales experience who want to first learn about and understand the Customer Success role. Cisco in general is an amazing company to work for and our leaders are just that; intelligent, committed, individuals who strive to ensure our success.

Customer Success is the new era of sales and I would highly reccomend this position. This role is unique in how it exposes you to the new way of not just selling products, but selling business outcomes. It's also exciting for those who like to innovate, value relationshipbuilding with the customer, and pioneer new processes and ideas. I really enjoy being able to have direct impact at a company this big and being a member of the Customer Success Team here at Cisco gives you that unique opportunity. 

I can't emphasize enough the responsiveness of our executives and leaders; I'm honestly amazed at how Cisco has given new employees the ability to have exposure with our senior management and how willing and compasionate they are about our sales team.

I would reccomend Cisco, Customer Success, and Sales to anyone, hands down.

Working at a fortune 100 company as large as Cisco, especially as we migrate our revenue model and product offerings, means there will be holes. I think this is natural at any large company but the mindset of adapting to everchanging processes, acquisitions, etc. is crucial in order to thrive. Not necessarily a con if you like a challenge and put in a lot of effort.

Pros: Interviewing with Bolt consisted of 45 conversations with leaders and stakeholders I'd be working alongside on a daily basis/supporting. Interviewers were engaging and it was a very positive experience overall. Once hired, onboarding took about 12 weeks and was very organized. Had more than enough support in terms of both materials and colleagues to get up to speed on Bolt's product, culture, etc. Pay and benefits are strong  company is remotefirst, Pay is competitive at/above industry average, and benefits are in alignment with other tech companies in the space. Despite previous restructures and changes in the organization the last few years, leaders are/have been transparent about the changes, the reasons behind them, and the vision/plan for Bolt moving forward. Product is interesting and a disrupter in the ecommerce space. You'll have the opportunity to work on/support the development of a product that supports well known brands everyone knows which is cool. There have been changes in leadership recently, and as a new hire, it seems from both a company vision/GTM strategy, as well as an employee morale standpoint, they are for the better. Individual contributors and leaders alike are aligned on the vision for the company and the product moving forward and are making a concerted effort to create a culture of more communication, transparency, and openness within all aspects of the organization. Definitely a startup culture where they prioritize hiring individuals who are able to/enjoy working autonomously, are strong culture builders, optimistic, and take ownership and accountability on the work they contribute. While there are more than enough systems/processes put in place, you also will have the opportunity to create processes from scratch or iterate on them. This may not be for everyone, but if you enjoy working in a high growth/scrappy startup environment, you will likely enjoy the type of work you get to do here.
Cons: Because of the multiple changes that have been made in the last 612 months, there may be some people that may not be aligned with the new vision/strategy of the company or new leadership moving forward. That being said, leadership has made a concerted effort to address this misalignment head on and have candid conversations about the future rather than not addressing people's apprehensions. From everything I've seen, department leaders and the executive team have taken a very humanistic approach to addressing people's concerns, and you can/will be heard and seen as a valued member of the Bolt organization.

Pros: Smart, collaborative people and an excellent executive leadership team Great market opportunity and strong company growth potential Anybody at the company can have outsize impact Cultural norms and tooling allow for teams and individuals to easily provide feedback positive & constructive to one another, and feedback is nearly always given appropriate consideration regardless of who is giving the feedback to whom. To that end, being successful at Bolt requires you to: Be highly thoughtful about what is a priority and what can be accomplished over a specific time frame, and be comfortable saying "no" to projects or goals that are unrealistic or not yet a priority.  Take time to build foundations, organizing information & data so that team members can make decisions quickly and then disseminate information about those decisions to key stakeholders with high efficiency.Currently, not every team or every individual makes the time to do the above on a regular basis, which can result in friction between teams and individuals.
